kp.k: Delivering legal work creates an automation feedback loop
kp.d: The founders describe Crosby as an AI-first law firm focused entirely on contracts, rather than a software vendor. They argue that delivering the work themselves, with lawyers sitting alongside engineers, supplies workflow knowledge, operational telemetry and detailed feedback beyond standalone evaluations or benchmarks. Their current scope is NDAs, MSAs and DPAs, not the entire range of legal services.
qs: So Crosby is an AI first law firm. We focus entirely on contracts.
So right now we focus on NDAs, MSAs, DPAs.
having your domain experts sit side by side with your engineers creates such a unique feedback loop where it's more than just eval.
we literally in our office have desks staggered lawyer engineer lawyer engineer

kp.k: Partnership economics inhibit speculative technology investment
kp.d: Daniels argues that traditional legal services prioritise human capital and that partnership financing constrains long-term technology investment. He cites accounting and consulting firms moving away from partnerships as an analogy, and Atrium and Clearspire as earlier attempts to combine legal services and technology. He attributes Crosby's opportunity to tighter lawyer-engineer coordination and newly delegable qualitative work; the transcript does not explain Crosby's precise ownership or regulatory arrangement.
qs: a law firm partnership, for example, doesn't allow you to invest in speculative things like building technology because you can't sell equity and only law firm partners can take loans that are recourse.
huge chunks of the qualitative uh thoughtful work that lawyers are doing each day can actually now be delegated to machines.

kp.k: Document pricing aligns incentives around efficiency
kp.d: The founders report rejecting hourly billing and charging by the document to align internal incentives with faster delivery. Daniels nevertheless considers hourly billing durable and suitable for sophisticated work whose demands cannot readily be predicted. Document pricing requires estimating the work and negotiation turns from the outset while maintaining quality and matching client value.
qs: what that looks like today is billing by the document
it makes a lot of sense for really sophisticated work where it's hard to x aanti predict how much work it will be.
being able to predict from time zero how long this piece of work is going to take so that we can price it

kp.k: Deal velocity defines the customer value proposition
kp.d: Daniels identifies deal velocity, rather than AI novelty alone, as the principal value for rapidly growing customers including Cursor and Clay. Crosby seeks both faster individual reviews and fewer negotiation rounds through selective, commercially informed objections. He reports median times a little under an hour and presents minutes as a goal, not an achieved result; these are founder-reported operational claims rather than independently documented measurements.

rather than doing five or six back and forths, we can sort of predict, okay, if we just agree to this term and only push back on these three, we're going to save one turn.

kp.d: Sarihan describes total turnaround time as Crosby's north-star metric, operationally summing the time Crosby spends on a contract across its negotiation rounds. The company also tracks human review time, touch points and service-level commitments. Responding to a host's concern that speed could sacrifice negotiating outcomes, he says lawyers and engineers focus specifically on quality, client risk profiles and negotiation interests as guardrails.

is this aligned with our customer's risk profile?

He argues that lawyer oversight and professional responsibility make AI-enabled delivery trustworthy. Crosby reports having malpractice insurance and accepting liability for its work. His expectation that lawyers remain involved in many legal tasks is a prediction, with accurate escalation to a lawyer central to the proposed model.

kp.d: Sarihan proposes first equipping human lawyers with the necessary context and workflow tools, then aligning models with the activities those lawyers perform. Because reasonable lawyers can disagree, he advocates alignment to an internally consistent individual and greater use of customer-specific evaluation, prompts and fine-tuning. His references to 90%, 99% and 99.99 accuracy illustrate the difficulty of improvement beyond initial performance, rather than report a Crosby test result or defined benchmark.

kp.d: The founders argue that foundation models lack sufficient representative contract data, describing SEC-filed EDGAR agreements as overused and poorly matched to smaller companies. They report that models struggle more than expected with legally consequential wording differences, leaving experienced lawyers responsible for actual edits. They also stress that product knowledge and client-specific business context are necessary, not merely general legal knowledge.

kp.k: Lawyers become prompt authors and workflow designers
kp.d: Daniels argues that explaining tacit expertise to AI will become a prized legal skill, contrasting it with apprenticeship through repetition. Crosby encourages lawyers to write prompts, articulate instructions and map processes, rewarding improvements that reduce review time rather than hours billed. He credits Harvey with providing a model through applied legal research roles, while presenting that attribution as his own belief. His advice to law students is to question established practices without dismissing legal scholarship and to learn how to harness AI.

kp.k: Repeatable work matters more than demand alone
kp.d: Sarihan warns that customers offering payment for additional tasks should not be mistaken for evidence of a scalable AI service. Providers must identify repeatable, automatable work and the signals that enable further automation. The founders connect this to autonomous multidisciplinary teams, with engineers working directly beside domain experts on shared outcomes, rather than shipping software without measuring operational results.

kp.k: Agent negotiations remain a future collaborative vision
kp.d: The founders envisage separate agents representing each party's preferences, simulating negotiation and producing an auditable sequence of exchanges for human consideration. They frame commercial contracting as collaborative rather than inherently adversarial and propose partitioned data and controlled communication between agents. Daniels also emphasises the continuing human contribution to reaching agreement; the discussion does not establish deployment of autonomous agent-to-agent negotiations.

kp.k: Access-to-justice automation is an explicitly optimistic prediction
kp.d: Daniels asserts that about 11,000 US law firms constitute 8% of firms and account for about 70–75% of revenue, while the remaining 92% serve individuals with needs such as leases and child support; no underlying study is supplied. He predicts complete automation for underserved individual legal needs because the alternative is often no assistance, while expecting corporate legal jobs to remain comparatively safe. He presents moving from two contracts per lawyer-hour to 500 as a hypothetical expansion of service capacity, not observed productivity.

kp.d: Asked about the industry in ten years, Sarihan imagines a senior associate managing many agents and expresses concern about opportunities for junior associates and paralegals. His personal-injury example places intake and demand-letter work within an agentic system while the human focuses on court appearances. This is a staffing forecast, not evidence of observed employment displacement, and differs in emphasis from Daniels's optimism about corporate legal jobs.

kp.k: In-house growth suggests opportunities for specialised AI providers
kp.d: Daniels states that in-house legal teams grew 200% during 2007–2017 while law firms grew 30%, and subsequently cites growth from about 320,000 to 440,000 during 2014–2024 without identifying the underlying source or precisely defining that count. He describes in-house teams as less constrained and more creative in combining lawyers, paralegals and legal operations. He reports increasing legal complexity as the prevailing explanation, then expresses hope that specialised AI-first providers will reshape delivery of work currently performed within corporate legal functions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Crosby's founders claim that delivering legal services themselves, with lawyers beside engineers, enables faster automation and richer feedback than selling software alone.
pts.d: Ryan Daniels describes Crosby as an AI-first law firm focused on contracts, seeking to automate negotiations by understanding lawyers' work and replacing as much of it agentically as possible. He argues that traditional partnership financing inhibits speculative technology investment, while a different structure enables iteration. John Sarihan says direct service delivery provides workflow observations, operational instrumentation and expert feedback beyond benchmarks. Their evidence is their own organisational experience, including staggered lawyer-engineer desks and faster progress after hiring more lawyers. These are present-tense operating claims and a broader prediction about AI-first service providers, not independently measured comparisons with conventional firms. Crosby is presented as a provider doing legal work, not merely a software vendor.

pts.k: AI-assisted contract work can increase deal velocity by shortening each review and reducing negotiation rounds.
pts.d: Daniels identifies deal velocity, rather than AI novelty alone, as Crosby's principal value proposition for rapidly growing businesses such as Cursor and Clay. He reports median contribution times slightly below an hour and asks whether they can reach minutes while routing the right terms to lawyers. He also claims that thoughtful AI-generated explanations encourage counterparties to accept changes, reducing turns; saving one turn is illustrated as potentially saving a week. Sarihan describes measuring cumulative Crosby review time across turns and human review time. The evidence is internal operating experience, including an observation dated only to 'about May'; no sample size or controlled customer-outcome study is supplied. Faster negotiation is conditional on quality, customer risk preferences and avoiding concessions that merely make signing easier.

pts.k: Document-based pricing aligns automation incentives, but requires predicting the work needed to complete a negotiation.
pts.d: Daniels says Crosby rejected hourly billing and currently bills by document. He connects this choice to incentives to reduce review time and to the need to estimate, from the outset, how many negotiation rounds a document will require. He does not predict universal or immediate disappearance of hourly billing: he calls it durable and appropriate for sophisticated work whose effort is hard to predict. The evidence is Crosby's own pricing practice and business-model reasoning, without disclosed prices, margins or comparative savings. The affected parties are Crosby's clients, lawyers and engineers, whose incentives differ from an hours-based service model.

pts.k: High-quality legal automation depends on client-specific context and expert preferences rather than general models alone.
pts.d: Sarihan argues for aligning systems with an individual lawyer's internally consistent judgments and for per-customer evaluation, prompting and fine-tuning, particularly for high-value customer relationships. His statement that models reach 90% easily but struggle to reach 99% or 99.99% is an illustrative reliability claim, not a reported legal benchmark result. Both founders describe limited access to relevant private contracts and difficulties with legally consequential wording. Sarihan identifies context engineering and reinforcement fine-tuning as promising routes, citing experiments in comment generation rather than validated general performance gains. Daniels says lawyers currently intervene on contract edits, while AI is particularly useful for summarisation and explanations. This is a present augmentation model with conditional ambitions for greater automation.

pts.k: Human lawyers will remain important as expert reviewers and bearers of professional responsibility for many legal services.
pts.d: Daniels argues that clients cannot readily judge legal quality themselves, so lawyer oversight makes AI-enabled services trustworthy. He predicts continued lawyer involvement for many kinds of work, with automation determining when to escalate issues for approval. He says Crosby has malpractice insurance and accepts liability for its work, treating that responsibility as essential to the business. This prediction is supported by his account of current practice and reasoning about client trust and liability, not evidence establishing a permanent technological limit. It is qualified by his separate prediction of full automation for some unmet individual legal needs.

pts.k: Agents may take over progressively more law-firm tasks, with reduced opportunities for junior associates and paralegals.
pts.d: Sarihan reports that Crosby has already built a paralegal-like agent that routes incoming work to human lawyers. He describes junior-associate, senior-associate and junior-partner functions as subsequent automation targets. In response to a ten-year outlook question, he imagines a senior associate managing an army of agents and expresses concern about junior associates and paralegals. His personal-injury example assigns intake and demand-letter workflows to agents, with the human principally appearing in court. Current routing automation is an operating claim; broader role substitution and employment effects are forecasts without staffing or displacement data. The increased 'leverage' here refers to agent-enabled capacity, not a reported associate-to-partner ratio.

pts.k: Explaining legal expertise, prompting and improving workflows will become valuable lawyer skills.
pts.d: Daniels predicts that explicitly teaching systems what lawyers know will become a prized capability, contrasting this with traditional apprenticeship through repeated practice. He describes lawyers writing prompts, giving instructions and mapping processes, and says Crosby rewards awareness of how work can be improved rather than hours billed alone. His evidence consists of workplace anecdotes, including a lawyer producing an extensive process map and weekly experiences of automating disliked tasks. The advice to current law students is to question inherited practices while respecting legal expertise and learn to harness AI; no formal training-outcome evidence or hiring projections are offered.

pts.k: AI could fully automate currently unmet individual legal needs, creating new access rather than simply replacing existing lawyers.
pts.d: Daniels predicts full automation of underserved individual matters such as leases and child-support issues because the alternative is often no assistance. He suggests people can already use ChatGPT for landlord-lease negotiations, while explicitly calling widespread present use a suspicion. He contrasts this with corporate law firms, which he expects to remain and whose jobs he calls relatively safe for quite a while. He cites an unsourced distribution claim that roughly 11,000 firms, or 8% of US firms, account for 70–75% of revenue, using the remaining long tail to motivate the access argument. His two-to-500-contracts-per-hour example is an aspiration about lawyer capacity, not demonstrated throughput. He labels the overall view an optimistic hot take and anticipates a golden age over the next five to ten years.

pts.k: Contract automation could quantify legal risk preferences and support auditable agent-to-agent negotiations.
pts.d: Daniels and Sarihan propose translating lawyers' heuristics about acceptable contract terms into probabilistic estimates informed by market data and business context. Daniels further describes a future in which each party's agents simulate negotiations and present an auditable sequence and proposed agreement for people to assess. Sarihan says separate agents' information must be partitioned and interactions constrained. These are prospective capabilities, not demonstrated market-wide risk metrics or deployed bilateral negotiation results. Daniels qualifies the vision by describing these negotiations as collaborative and preserving an essential human role in reaching agreement.

pts.k: Specialised AI-first providers may change legal delivery as corporate legal functions expand.
pts.d: In the ten-year outlook discussion, Daniels points to expanding in-house legal departments and their ability to combine lawyers, paralegals and legal operations. He hopes more specialised AI-first companies will deliver legal services, rather than corporations simply expanding functions outside their core business. He cites 200% in-house-team growth versus 30% law-firm growth during 2007–2017, followed by a rise from about 320,000 to 440,000 during 2014–2024 in the same discussion. No sources or precise population definitions are supplied. These historical figures motivate, but are distinct from, his forward-looking hope; he does not quantify future market shares or outsourcing volumes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main evidence offered is founder-reported operational experience, supplemented by unsourced market figures and explicitly speculative scenarios.
pts.d: Present operating claims include work-routing agents, document pricing, lawyer oversight, malpractice coverage, median contribution times and reinforcement fine-tuning experiments. Workplace anecdotes support claims about feedback loops, explanation quality and new lawyer skills. Market statistics support the access-to-justice and in-house-growth narratives but are not sourced in the transcript.
